title: Add each file's date as a prefix to its name
summary: Puts the date a file was last changed in front of its name, for example 2024-03-05_photo.jpg. Files whose name already starts with a date are left alone. You see the planned names first, then apply them.

steps.explain: Preview only: print the planned move for each plain file. The date comes from the file's modification time (date -r reads it), in your local time zone. Files that already start with a date are skipped.
steps.cmd: (cd <DIR> && for f in *; do [ -f "$f" ] || continue; case "$f" in ????-??-??_*) continue ;; esac; printf 'mv -- %q %q\n' "$f" "$(date -r "$f" +%F)_$f"; done)
steps.expect: Lines such as: mv -- photo\ one.jpg 2024-03-05_photo\ one.jpg

steps.explain: Apply the new names. mv -n never overwrites an existing file, so a name clash leaves the file unchanged.
steps.cmd: (cd <DIR> && for f in *; do [ -f "$f" ] || continue; case "$f" in ????-??-??_*) continue ;; esac; mv -n -- "$f" "$(date -r "$f" +%F)_$f"; done)
steps.expect: No output. The files now start with their date.

placeholders.name: DIR
placeholders.description: Same folder as in the preview step

steps.expect: Each name starts with YYYY-MM-DD_ followed by the old name.

rollback.explain: Remove the date prefix again. The preview output lists every old and new name, so reverse each pair with mv.

warnings: The date is the modification time, not the date a photo was taken, even though the aliases mention shooting date. Copying or editing a file changes it.
Run the apply step only once per file; files that already start with a date are skipped by the check.
Names are in your local time zone, so files changed near midnight can get the next day's date.
